stem:
The neonatal team is preparing to stabilise a baby about to be born at 27 weeks. A preheated radiant warmer and respiratory support equipment are ready.

Which immediate thermal measure is recommended in addition to the warmer?

options.label: A
options.text: Dry the body thoroughly first, then apply the polyethylene wrap
options.explanation: For a very preterm baby, drying the body before wrapping is unnecessary and can increase heat loss. The wrap is applied immediately while the body is still wet.

options.label: B
options.text: Place the wet body in polyethylene up to the neck and add a hat
options.explanation: A suitable polyethylene bag or sheet limits evaporative heat loss without prior body drying. Keep the face accessible, use a warm hat and monitor temperature during stabilisation.

options.label: C
options.text: Wrap the body in a dry cotton towel instead of polyethylene
options.explanation: A towel is used routinely for more mature babies, but is less effective at limiting evaporative loss from the immature skin of a very preterm baby.

options.label: D
options.text: Leave the body uncovered to maximise exposure to radiant heat
options.explanation: A radiant warmer alone does not adequately address the large evaporative losses of very preterm skin. A transparent polyethylene barrier can be used under the warmer.

options.label: E
options.text: Delay any wrapping until respiratory stabilisation is complete
options.explanation: Thermal protection should begin immediately and continue during respiratory support. Waiting through stabilisation permits avoidable heat loss.

context: Very preterm babies need immediate polyethylene wrapping without drying the body, alongside a radiant warmer and temperature monitoring.
